subject: ela
intro: Each item below gives you a full short presentation, an outline, or a transcript with a delivery note. Read the whole scenario, then evaluate it as a whole. Decide what works, what does not, and which single change would most improve the speaker's claim and findings.

items.prompt: Read this transcript of Maya's presentation about starting a school garden. 'Our school should plant a garden behind the gym. Right now that space is just dirt and weeds that nobody uses. A garden would give students fresh vegetables for the cafeteria, and a teacher said it could be used for science lessons too. My older sister loves gardening and has a really nice greenhouse at home. Two other schools in our district built gardens last year and reported that students ate more vegetables. So a garden would help both our health and our learning.' One sentence weakens this otherwise strong presentation. Identify that sentence, explain why it does not belong, and state what the speaker should do.
items.answer: The sentence 'My older sister loves gardening and has a really nice greenhouse at home' weakens the presentation because it is a personal note that does not support the claim that the school should plant a garden, and it should be cut.

steps: Find the claim: the school should plant a garden behind the gym.
Check each detail against that claim. The unused space, fresh vegetables, science lessons, and the two district schools all support the claim with relevant facts.
The sentence about the older sister's greenhouse is about one family member's hobby, not about whether the school needs or would benefit from a garden, so it is off topic.
Because a presentation is stronger when every detail supports the claim, the speaker should remove that sentence rather than keep it just to add length.

items.prompt: Read this outline a student wrote for a presentation, listed in the order he plans to say it: (1) 'Here is my plan: add a covered rack with twenty spaces near the front door.' (2) 'Our school should build a safe place to park bikes.' (3) 'Last month eight bikes were left leaning against the fence in the rain.' (4) 'A nearby school added a bike rack and saw twice as many students ride to school.' The student is happy with the plan but unsure of the order. Give the most logical order of the four points and explain why that order works best.
items.answer: The most logical order is 2, 3, 4, 1. The speaker should state the claim, show the current problem, give evidence that a solution works, then present the specific plan.

steps: Identify the claim, point 2, which tells the audience the main position up front.
After the claim, point 3 shows the problem that makes the claim necessary, the bikes left in the rain.
Point 4 then offers evidence that a bike rack works, using the nearby school's result.
Point 1, the detailed plan, comes last because a plan makes the most sense after the audience accepts the claim, the problem, and the evidence.
This order, 2, 3, 4, 1, builds from claim to problem to proof to plan, which is more logical than leading with the plan or the most dramatic fact.

items.prompt: Read this description of Daniel's presentation about school lunches. 'Daniel had accurate facts and a clear claim that the cafeteria should offer a salad bar. However, he stared down at his note cards the whole time and never looked at the audience. He also rushed through his sentences so quickly that several listeners said they missed his main point.' A classmate says, 'His presentation was effective because all his facts were correct.' Explain why the classmate's judgment is incomplete and name the two delivery features Daniel most needs to fix.
items.answer: The classmate is judging only content and ignoring delivery. Even with correct facts, Daniel's presentation was hard to follow, so it was not fully effective. He most needs to improve his eye contact and his pace, looking up at the audience and slowing down so listeners can follow him.

steps: A presentation is judged on both content and delivery, not content alone.
Daniel's content is strong: a clear claim and accurate facts.
His delivery is weak: he never looked up, which is an eye contact problem, and he rushed so listeners missed the point, which is a pace problem.
Because delivery problems stopped the audience from following him, the classmate's claim that the presentation was effective is incomplete.
The two features to fix are eye contact, by looking up at the audience, and pace, by slowing down to speak clearly.

items.prompt: Read this transcript of Priya presenting about recess time. 'Sixth graders should get a longer recess. Studies of schools that added ten minutes of recess found students focused better in afternoon classes. Recess also lets students get exercise during the day. My favorite part of recess is playing four square with my friends. Teachers in those studies also reported fewer behavior problems after recess was extended.' Priya's claim and most details are strong, but one revision would improve the presentation most. Choose and justify the single best revision: (A) Add more sentences about four square. (B) Remove the sentence 'My favorite part of recess is playing four square with my friends.' (C) Move the claim to the end. (D) Delete the studies because they are boring.
items.answer: B) Remove the sentence 'My favorite part of recess is playing four square with my friends.' It is a personal preference that does not support the claim that sixth graders should get a longer recess, while the studies and exercise points do support it.

steps: The claim is that sixth graders should get a longer recess.
The studies on focus, the exercise benefit, and the fewer behavior problems all support that claim with relevant findings.
The four square sentence is a personal preference, not evidence that recess should be longer, so it is the off topic detail.
Option A adds more off topic material, option C breaks the logical order, and option D removes the strongest evidence, so they are wrong.
Option B keeps the findings focused and is the single best revision.

items.prompt: Read this presentation transcript about phone use. 'Our class should be allowed to use phones for research during projects. Phones can quickly look up facts we need. A survey of our class showed twenty out of twenty-five students wanted this. Phones are also fun to play games on during free time. A teacher said supervised phone use helped her last class find sources faster.' Identify the one detail that does not support the claim, explain why it actually works against the speaker's purpose, and tell what to do with it.
items.answer: The detail 'Phones are also fun to play games on during free time' does not support the claim about using phones for research. It works against the speaker's purpose because it suggests phones are a distraction, which gives the audience a reason to say no, so the speaker should remove it.

steps: The claim is narrow: phones should be allowed for research during projects.
The quick lookups, the class survey, and the teacher's report all support that specific claim.
The detail about games is about entertainment, not research, so it does not support the claim.
Worse, it reminds the audience that phones can distract, which undercuts the speaker's own purpose of getting research approved.
The speaker should cut that detail so every point keeps the focus on research.

items.prompt: Read this outline for a presentation arguing that the library should stay open after school, listed in the order planned: (1) 'My plan is to keep the library open until 4:30 with one staff member.' (2) 'Some students have nowhere quiet to do homework after school.' (3) 'The library should stay open later so students have a place to study.' (4) 'When a nearby school extended library hours, more students finished homework on time.' The speaker wants the most logical order. Give the best order and explain why leading with the plan, as the speaker first planned, is a weaker choice.
items.answer: The best order is 3, 2, 4, 1: state the claim, show the problem, give the supporting evidence, then present the plan. Leading with the plan is weaker because the audience does not yet understand the claim or the problem the plan is meant to solve.

steps: Point 3 is the claim and belongs first so the audience knows the speaker's position.
Point 2 shows the problem, students having nowhere quiet to study, which makes the claim matter.
Point 4 provides evidence that the idea works, using the nearby school's result.
Point 1, the specific plan, fits best at the end after the audience accepts the claim, problem, and evidence.
Leading with the plan, as first written, asks the audience to consider a solution before they understand why it is needed, which breaks the logical flow.

items.prompt: Read this description of two speakers presenting the same claim, that the school should add a homework help club. 'Liam spoke at a good volume and looked at the audience, but he had only one vague reason: clubs are good. Sofia had three specific facts, including a survey result and a teacher quote, but she mumbled so quietly that the back rows could not hear her.' A judge must pick which presentation needs the bigger fix and say what that fix is. Explain which speaker has the more serious problem and what single change would help that speaker most.
items.answer: Liam has the more serious problem because his content is weak: one vague reason does not support the claim. The single change that would help him most is to add specific, relevant facts, such as a survey result or expert quote, to support the claim. Sofia's issue is volume, which is a real but more easily fixed delivery problem.

steps: Judge both content and delivery for each speaker.
Liam's delivery is fine, but his support is one vague opinion, which is a content weakness that leaves the claim unsupported.
Sofia's content is strong with three specific facts; her only issue is volume, a delivery problem fixed by speaking louder.
A claim with no real support is a deeper problem than a strong case spoken too quietly.
So Liam needs the bigger fix: add specific, relevant supporting facts to back the claim.

items.prompt: Read this transcript about a class recycling project. 'Our class should run the school recycling bins this year. Last year the bins overflowed because no one emptied them. Our class is responsible and has free time during fourth period. Recycling helps reduce waste in landfills. The principal said she would support a student-led recycling team. Also, my brother is on the high school recycling team.' Two things could be improved: the order is fine, but one detail is off topic and the speaker buries the strongest point. Identify the off topic detail and name which remaining point is the strongest support for the claim.
items.answer: The off topic detail is 'Also, my brother is on the high school recycling team,' because a relative's activity does not show that this class should run the bins. The strongest support for the claim is that the principal said she would support a student-led recycling team, since it shows the plan is approved and feasible.

steps: The claim is that this class should run the school recycling bins.
The overflowing bins, the class's free time, the landfill benefit, and the principal's support all relate to the claim.
The brother on the high school team is about a relative, not about this class running the bins, so it is the off topic detail to cut.
Among the relevant points, the principal's support is strongest because it shows the plan is both approved and possible, which an audience needs to accept the claim.
So cut the brother detail and lean on the principal's support.

items.prompt: Read this transcript about water fountains. 'The school should install two new water fountains in the science wing. Right now there is only one fountain for that whole wing, and lines form between classes. A nurse said staying hydrated helps students concentrate. New fountains can also refill water bottles, which cuts down on plastic waste. The science wing has the most classrooms of any wing in the building.' Which single revision would most improve this presentation: (A) Cut the sentence about the nurse and hydration. (B) Cut the sentence 'The science wing has the most classrooms of any wing in the building.' (C) Keep all sentences because more details are always better. (D) Move the claim to the end of the presentation. Choose and justify your answer.
items.answer: C) Keep all sentences because each one supports the claim, but note that this is the best choice only because no detail is off topic; the presentation does not need a cut. Every sentence here, the single fountain and lines, the nurse on hydration, the bottle refilling, and the science wing having the most classrooms, supports installing two new fountains, so the presentation is already focused.

steps: The claim is that the school should install two new fountains in the science wing.
Check each detail: the lines show need, the nurse's point shows benefit, bottle refilling shows added value, and the most classrooms point shows why this wing needs them most.
Because every detail supports the claim, cutting any of them, options A and B, would remove relevant evidence.
Moving the claim to the end, option D, breaks the logical order, so it is wrong.
Option C is correct here: keep all sentences, since this is one of the cases where each detail truly is relevant, not because more is automatically better.

items.prompt: Read this description of Ava's presentation about a class trip. 'Ava argued the class should visit the science museum. She had strong, relevant facts and a clear claim. But she read every word straight from her paper without ever looking up, and she pronounced several key terms so unclearly that listeners could not tell whether she said "fossils" or "forests." Her volume was perfectly fine.' A classmate says Ava should practice speaking louder. Explain why that advice misnames the problem and state the two delivery features Ava actually needs to improve.
items.answer: The advice is wrong because Ava's volume was already fine, so speaking louder fixes nothing. Her real delivery problems are eye contact, since she never looked up from her paper, and pronunciation, since listeners could not tell which words she said. She should look up at the audience and pronounce key terms clearly.

steps: Identify what the description actually says about delivery.
Volume is described as perfectly fine, so the classmate's advice to be louder misnames the problem.
Never looking up from the paper is an eye contact problem.
Saying terms so unclearly that listeners cannot tell the words apart is a pronunciation problem, not a volume problem.
So Ava needs to improve eye contact and pronunciation, not volume.

items.prompt: Read this transcript about a school newspaper. 'Our school should bring back the student newspaper. A newspaper gives students a way to share news and practice writing. Test scores rose by twelve points at a school with a newspaper. The old newspaper ended three years ago when the advisor retired. A new English teacher has offered to advise the club.' A student says, 'The claim of this presentation is that test scores rose by twelve points.' Explain why that student has confused the claim with a supporting detail, and state what the actual claim is.
items.answer: The student confused a supporting fact for the claim. 'Test scores rose by twelve points' is a specific fact offered to support the position, not the position itself. The actual claim is that the school should bring back the student newspaper.

steps: A claim is the speaker's main position; supporting details are the facts that back it up.
'Our school should bring back the student newspaper' tells the audience what the speaker wants, so it is the claim.
'Test scores rose by twelve points' is a specific statistic that gives a reason to agree, which makes it a supporting detail, not the main point.
Mistaking a confident-sounding statistic for the claim is a common error.
So the actual claim is that the school should bring back the student newspaper.

items.prompt: Read this outline for a presentation that the cafeteria should offer a vegetarian option, in the planned order: (1) 'A survey found one in four students would choose a vegetarian meal at least twice a week.' (2) 'The cafeteria should add a daily vegetarian main dish.' (3) 'Right now students who do not eat meat often have only a side salad to choose from.' (4) 'The food service manager said adding one vegetarian dish would not raise costs much.' The speaker placed the survey statistic first because it is the most striking. Explain why opening with the statistic weakens the logic and give the stronger order.
items.answer: Opening with the statistic weakens the logic because the audience hears a number before they know the claim or the problem it relates to. The stronger order is 2, 3, 1, 4: state the claim, show the problem, give the survey evidence, then add the cost reassurance.

steps: Point 2 is the claim and should come first so listeners know the position.
Point 3 shows the problem, that vegetarian students often have only a side salad.
Point 1, the survey, then supplies evidence of demand, which now makes sense because the audience understands the claim and problem.
Point 4, the manager's note on cost, fits last to remove a likely objection.
Leading with the striking statistic, as planned, drops a number on the audience before the claim, which is ordering by drama instead of logic and weakens the flow.

items.prompt: Read this transcript about after-school sports. 'More sixth graders should join after-school sports. Sports build teamwork and keep students active. A coach reported that students in sports had better attendance. I think running is the most fun sport of all. Joining a team also helps students make new friends.' Then read this delivery note: 'The speaker looked up at the audience and spoke clearly, but talked so softly that half the room could not hear.' This presentation has both a content issue and a delivery issue. Name each issue and state the single revision that would most improve the content.
items.answer: The content issue is the off topic sentence 'I think running is the most fun sport of all,' a personal opinion that does not support the claim. The delivery issue is volume, since half the room could not hear. The single content revision that would most improve the presentation is to remove that personal opinion so the remaining facts stay focused on the claim.

steps: The claim is that more sixth graders should join after-school sports.
Teamwork and activity, the coach's attendance report, and making new friends all support the claim.
'I think running is the most fun sport of all' is a personal opinion about one sport, not support for the claim, so it is the content issue.
The delivery note says the speaker was too soft, so volume is the delivery issue.
The single best content revision is to remove the personal opinion, keeping the supporting details relevant; the speaker should also speak louder to fix delivery.

items.prompt: Read this transcript about a class pet. 'Our classroom should get a pet fish. A fish is calm and easy to care for. Caring for a pet can teach students responsibility. A science teacher said observing a fish could support our unit on living things. Fish tanks look nice. I once had a dog named Rex who could do tricks.' The speaker has a clear claim but included weak support. Identify the two sentences that provide the weakest support, and for each explain whether it is off topic or just too vague.
items.answer: The two weakest sentences are 'I once had a dog named Rex who could do tricks,' which is off topic because a past dog does not support getting a classroom fish, and 'Fish tanks look nice,' which is too vague because it is a general opinion that does not give a specific reason the class needs a fish.

steps: The claim is that the classroom should get a pet fish.
Being calm and easy to care for, teaching responsibility, and supporting the living things unit are specific, relevant reasons.
'I once had a dog named Rex who could do tricks' is about a past pet dog, unrelated to getting a classroom fish, so it is off topic.
'Fish tanks look nice' shares the topic but is a vague opinion with no specific reason, so it is too vague to count as strong support.
The strong support stays; both weak sentences should be cut or replaced with specific facts.

items.prompt: Read this full short presentation about a buddy reading program. 'Our school should start a buddy reading program where sixth graders read with first graders. Younger students who read with older buddies in other schools improved their reading scores. The first grade teachers have said they would welcome the help. It only takes twenty minutes a week. Also, the gym floor was just repainted and looks great. Sixth graders would build leadership skills by mentoring.' Then read this delivery note: 'The speaker had good eye contact and clear pronunciation but spoke too quietly to be heard in the back.' Choose the single revision that would most improve this presentation and justify it: (A) Speak louder and leave the content as is. (B) Cut the sentence about the repainted gym floor, since it is the off topic detail. (C) Move the claim to the end. (D) Remove the fact about reading scores because numbers are boring.
items.answer: B) Cut the sentence about the repainted gym floor, since it is the off topic detail. The repainted gym floor has nothing to do with a buddy reading program, while every other detail supports the claim; cutting it keeps the findings focused. The speaker should also speak louder, but the single revision that most improves the presentation itself is removing the off topic sentence.

steps: The claim is that the school should start a buddy reading program.
The reading-score evidence, the teachers' welcome, the small time commitment, and the leadership benefit all support the claim.
'The gym floor was just repainted and looks great' is unrelated to reading, so it is the off topic detail.
Option A ignores that off topic sentence, option C breaks the logical order, and option D removes the strongest evidence, so all three are wrong.
Option B removes the off topic sentence and most improves the presentation; the volume problem from the delivery note should also be fixed by speaking louder.
